newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Dunblane father urges Australia to ban handguns.
newsitem.headline: Dunblane father urges Australia to ban handguns.

text.p: The father of a child who was killed in the Dunblane massacre urged Australia on Friday to impose tougher gun control laws, despite legislative changes already made after last year's killing spree in Port Arthur.

Les Morton told a news conference that Australian should consider banning handguns because the current laws are similar to those in existence in Britain before lone gunman Thomas Hamilton murdered 17 people last year before killing himself.
"The handgun law in Australia is as it was (in Britain) on March 13 last year and that means that any person armed to the teeth could do something unpredictable," Morton said.
Hamilton walked into a school in the quiet Scottish town with four handguns and 743 rounds of ammunition and murdered 16 children, including Morton's five-year-old daughter Emily.
Britain responded to the massacre by banning hand guns above .22 calibre, while Australia concentrated on changing laws relating to automatic and semi-automatic weapons.
Martin Bryant, 29, used high-powered semi-automatic rifles when he killed 35 people among the ruins of the former convict settlement on April 28 last year.
"We're not here to tell you what your laws should be but we urge you to be tough on gun control," Morton said.
"My daughter was murdered with a handgun. These things can and do kill," he said.
New South Wales state premier Bob Carr told the news conference he regarded self-loading weapons as the major problem but added he would listen to suggestions regarding handguns.
"Any representation about more effective policing of handguns will be listened to by the government," Carr said.

Morton and two other Dunblane victims' fathers, Gordon Bounds and John Crozier, are in Australia to offer support to the families of Port Arthur victims ahead of the Australian massacre's first anniversary.
They launched a campaign urging Australians to mark the Port Arthur anniversary by lighting candles on April 28 as Britons had done last month to commemorate Dunblane victims.

Carr donated A$6,000 (US$4,620) to an Australian victims support group and urged British prime minister John Major and opposition leader Tony Blair to do the same for such groups in the United Kingdom.
